title: Strategic Thinking
description: Editable version of the complete Mayne Leadership Strategic Thinking course, including its original explanations, practice activities, application, and reflection prompts.
author: Joshua Mayne

blocks.body: Strategic thinking changes the frame. It expands the time horizon, widens the stakeholder view, tests assumptions, and considers the consequences of action before the system makes them visible.
See More → Think Deeper → Look Further → Lead Broader.
Approx. 2 hours · Interactive self-paced course · Progress saved on this device

This online version follows the full two-hour Strategic Thinking module: first expand the frame, then build the six competencies, examine the habits that enable or block strategic judgment, test assumptions, connect decisions through time, and finish with a systems capstone.
What you will practice

Expand the frame
Move beyond the visible problem and identify what else is connected.

Use six competencies
Information gathering, learning, critical thinking, innovative thinking, thinking in time, and systems thinking.

Protect judgment
Recognize blockers, cognitive biases, fallacies, assumptions, and the Ladder of Inference.

Test strategy
Use Ends–Ways–Means–Risk and first-, second-, and third-order effects.

Integrate the system
Finish with a strategic systems challenge and personal transfer plan.

blocks.title: Better problem framing before solution jumping.

blocks.body: Strategic thinking is not just a larger version of tactical thinking. It changes the time horizon, number of stakeholders, amount of ambiguity, and consequences of being wrong.
Approx. 2 hours

A regional office faces a 35% workload increase. Temporary resources are authorized. Leaders are considering shifting personnel away from training and long-term initiatives to meet the immediate demand.
What is your first judgment?

blocks.title: Now widen the frame.
blocks.body:
Choose the option or options that best fit your situation and explain your reasoning.

  • Good decision
  • Bad decision
  • Not enough information

items.title: Reveal information 1
items.text: Training completion is already below target.

items.title: Reveal information 2
items.text: Overtime is rising and experienced supervisors are nearing retirement.

items.title: Reveal information 3
items.text: A major technology modernization begins in four months.

items.title: Reveal information 4
items.text: Senior leadership has requested additional performance information.

blocks.body: Did the problem change—or did your understanding change? Strategic thinking often begins when we recognize that our first frame was too small.
Strategic thinking improves action by preventing us from solving the wrong problem quickly.
IT IS
Seeing relationships
Look for assumptions, trends, stakeholders, dependencies, consequences, choices, and future conditions.
IT IS NOT
Vague forecasting
It is not jargon, endless brainstorming, or pretending to predict the distant future with certainty.
ANY LEVEL
A practice, not a position
You can think strategically without holding a “strategic” title. The behavior begins with how you frame decisions.
Tactical thinking asks: “How do we solve today’s visible problem?” Strategic thinking also asks: “What created it, what else is connected, where are we trying to go, and what might happen next?”

blocks.title: The question changes as the level expands.

blocks.body: Open all four levels. Notice how the same staffing issue becomes a different problem depending on the horizon.

items.title: IMMEDIATE
items.text: Task or incident — Who covers today’s requirement?

items.title: DIRECT
items.text: People and team — How does the team adjust workload without creating avoidable failure?

items.title: ORGANIZATIONAL
items.text: Systems and resources — Is the staffing model, training pipeline, and process sustainable?

items.title: STRATEGIC
items.text: Enterprise and future conditions — What future capability must be built, and what tradeoffs today shape it?

blocks.title: Almost nothing important happens in isolation.

blocks.body: A decision made in one part of an organization can create pressure, opportunity, delay, or unintended effects somewhere else. Strategic thinkers look for these connections before choosing action.
Mission / Operations
Workforce
Training & Learning
Legal / Policy
Technology
Resources / Budget
Partners
Customers / Public
Ask: Where have you seen one part of a system make a decision that created pressure somewhere else?

blocks.title: Four habits organize the whole course.

blocks.body: Open each element to see the question it contributes.

items.title: SEE MORE
items.text: Gather perspectives and evidence. — Whose information is missing? What are we not seeing?

items.title: THINK DEEPER
items.text: Challenge assumptions and causality. — What would have to be true for this recommendation to work?

items.title: LOOK FURTHER
items.text: Anticipate consequences and future conditions. — What happens next—and what happens because of that?

items.title: LEAD BROADER
items.text: Align beyond your immediate control. — Who must understand, contribute, or change behavior?

blocks.body: These are habits—not personality traits. Open all six.

items.title: Information Gathering
items.text: Scan broadly before deciding narrowly. Seek facts, perspectives, constraints, and dissenting information.

items.title: Learning
items.text: Update the mental model. Treat feedback as information and build reflection into routine work.

items.title: Critical Thinking
items.text: Challenge assumptions and causal claims. Distinguish causes from symptoms and consequences.

items.title: Innovative Thinking
items.text: Create multiple ways before choosing one. Reframe constraints and generate disciplined alternatives.

items.title: Thinking in Time
items.text: Connect Then → Now → Next. Use history, current conditions, and plausible futures together.

items.title: Systems Thinking
items.text: Look for dependencies, bottlenecks, incentives, feedback, and unintended effects.

blocks.body: The competencies are strongest when used together: gather broadly, learn and update, test the logic, create alternatives, connect past-present-future, and examine the system.

blocks.title: Good tools still fail without good habits.

blocks.body: Select the three enablers you believe are most difficult to sustain when pressure is high.
BROAD KNOWLEDGE

You do not need to be an expert in everything. You need enough range to recognize dependencies and ask intelligent questions about people, policy, law, technology, resources, partners, and other functions.
COLLABORATION + COMMUNICATION
Collaboration is more than passing tasks between groups. It means jointly making sense of the problem. Communication then turns complexity into usable meaning without hiding important tradeoffs.
COURAGE + REGULATION + ETHICS
Moral courage helps leaders say what needs to be heard. Emotional regulation keeps thinking open when challenged. Ethical reasoning asks “should we?” along with “can we?”
Now choose the three enablers you believe are hardest to sustain under pressure.

blocks.title: Three habits to strengthen
blocks.body:
Choose three enablers you most need to strengthen and explain how you will practice them.

  • Broad knowledge
  • Collaboration
  • Communication
  • Moral courage
  • Emotional regulation
  • Ethical reasoning
  • Self-awareness

Strategic thinking is not purely cognitive. Curiosity, collaboration, communication, courage, emotional regulation, ethical reasoning, and self-awareness determine whether good questions actually get asked.

blocks.title: Where is your strategic-thinking edge—and blind spot?

blocks.body: Rate each statement from 1 (rarely) to 5 (consistently). Your scores stay on this device.

blocks.title: I seek information that contradicts my first position.
I separate facts from interpretation and assumptions.
I consider second- and third-order effects.
I can explain how my team’s work connects to broader outcomes.
I revise my view when new evidence changes the picture.
ONE STRENGTH
blocks.body: Which behavior is already a strength?

blocks.title: ONE BLIND SPOT
blocks.body: Where might others see a gap you miss?

blocks.title: ONE PRACTICE TARGET
blocks.body: What behavior will you deliberately practice?
The number is less important than the pattern. The goal is to identify one behavior to practice deliberately rather than trying to “be more strategic” in the abstract.
Pressure makes certainty feel attractive. Strategic thinkers make assumptions visible enough to examine.

blocks.title: Most barriers are habits under pressure.

blocks.body: Select the two blockers most likely to distort a difficult decision.

blocks.title: Two strategic-thinking barriers
blocks.body:
Choose two barriers most relevant to your work and explain what you will do about them.

  • Expertise trap — Past success becomes the only lens for the next problem.
  • Tactical gravity — Urgency consumes all attention and pushes long-term conditions out of view.
  • Silos & conformity — The frame is built inside one lane and dissent disappears.
  • Certainty hunger — Ambiguity feels unacceptable, so the first plausible explanation hardens too quickly.

Strong leaders often overuse strengths that made them successful: expertise becomes rigidity, responsiveness becomes tactical gravity, decisiveness becomes premature closure, and loyalty becomes conformity.
Bias is rarely obvious while it is happening. Select at least one that you want to watch for in your own decisions.

items.back: We search for or favor evidence that supports the preferred view.
The first number, explanation, or proposal shapes later judgment.
Recent or vivid examples feel more common or important than they may be.
The familiar option feels safer simply because it is familiar.
Past investment keeps us committed even when conditions have changed.
Harmony and belonging crowd out examination or dissent.
The way a problem is presented changes which options seem reasonable.
We judge the quality of a decision mainly by how it turned out.

blocks.body: Countermeasure: Name the bias before it names the decision. Deliberately seek disconfirming evidence, alternate frames, or an outside perspective.
Fallacies can make weak reasoning sound stronger than it is. Select at least one you want to catch in meetings, briefings, or written recommendations.

items.back: Two choices are presented as if no other alternatives exist.
A limited example becomes a broad conclusion.
Because B followed A, we assume A caused B.
A claim is treated as sound mainly because an authority said it.
An opposing view is weakened or distorted before being rejected.
One change is treated as inevitably leading to an extreme outcome.

blocks.body: Countermeasure: Slow the argument down and test the actual claim. Ask what evidence supports it, what alternatives exist, and whether the conclusion follows from the premise.

blocks.title: Turn a conclusion back into a testable assumption.

blocks.body: “Employees are resisting because they do not like change.”
What hidden assumption is embedded in that statement?

blocks.title: Name the hidden assumption...
blocks.body: Name the hidden assumption...
What evidence would confirm or challenge it?

blocks.title: Name one useful piece of evidence...
blocks.body: Name one useful piece of evidence...
Assumptions are not automatically bad. Untested assumptions are dangerous. The strategic habit is to make them visible before they become conclusions, beliefs, and action.
Strategy is not prediction. It is preparing decisions to survive changing conditions.

blocks.title: If the ends exceed the means, the ways may be a wish.

blocks.body: Use the workload scenario to create a simple strategic check.

blocks.title: ENDS · Desired condition
blocks.body: What condition are we trying to create?

blocks.title: WAYS · Broad approach
blocks.body: What broad approach could move us there?

blocks.title: MEANS · Resources and authorities
blocks.body: People, time, money, authorities, technology, partnerships...

blocks.title: RISK · Friction and consequences
blocks.body: What could fail or what harm could the approach create?
A strategy becomes more credible when the desired condition, approach, resources, and risk are visible together rather than discussed as separate ideas.
Choose a proposed decision—such as shifting personnel away from training—and identify what happens next.
FIRST-ORDER EFFECT
The immediate result.

blocks.title: What changes immediately?
blocks.body: What changes immediately?
SECOND-ORDER EFFECT
What happens because of that result?

blocks.title: What consequence follows?
blocks.body: What consequence follows?
THIRD-ORDER EFFECT
How might the broader system respond?

blocks.title: What changes later or elsewhere?
blocks.body: What changes later or elsewhere?
Thinking in time connects Then → Now → Next. It helps leaders use history without being trapped by it and consider future effects without pretending the future is certain.
At the strategic level, almost nothing important happens in isolation.

blocks.title: Map the system before recommending action.

blocks.body: Imagine that workload is rising, experienced employees are retiring, technology modernization is accelerating, partner capacity is uneven, and workforce expectations are changing. Do not solve everything. Build a better strategic picture.

blocks.title: 3 CRITICAL CONNECTIONS
blocks.body: What variables, groups, or systems are strongly connected?

blocks.title: 2 ASSUMPTIONS
blocks.body: What are leaders treating as true that needs testing?

blocks.title: 2 SECOND-ORDER EFFECTS
blocks.body: What happens because of the immediate effects?

blocks.title: 1 STRATEGIC RISK + 1 OPPORTUNITY
blocks.body: What could worsen? What could be leveraged?

blocks.title: 1 SENIOR-LEADER QUESTION
blocks.body: What question would improve the decision before action?

The purpose of strategic thinking is not to produce a perfect map. It is to understand enough of the system to ask better questions, make better tradeoffs, and anticipate where action may create pressure elsewhere.
